kurz: How need, Social Security and other entitlements, assets and savings contribution are calculated on a consistent basis, in which order to save, and what plans for 30-, 45- and 55-year-olds look like.

bloecke.md:
A retirement plan is an equation with four quantities: need in retirement, entitlements already acquired, existing assets and the savings contribution still required. Whether the end result is a 401(k), an IRA, a brokerage account or an annuity is only the second question. If you reverse the order, you may have a product, but you still do not know whether it is enough.

The equation fits on one page. However, it only holds if all four quantities are expressed in the same unit, that is, in the same purchasing power, at the same point in time and after tax rather than before. Most private rough calculations fail on this condition. If a gross benefit is deducted from an after-tax need, or a gap calculated in today's dollars is closed with a nominal return, the result comes out systematically too favorable, and by an order of magnitude that corresponds to decades of saving.

bloecke.titel: Calculating in real or nominal terms
bloecke.md: Either everything is calculated in real terms (today's purchasing power, real return, savings contribution increased annually by inflation) or everything in nominal terms (need compounded forward, nominal return, fixed savings contribution). Mixing the two is the most common and most expensive mistake in retirement planning. This lesson calculates in real terms throughout.

## Taking stock (step 1)

Before any estimate, the documents are gathered. Most entitlements in the US are reported regularly or can be called up online. The difficulty therefore lies less in obtaining them than in the fact that the documents are kept in different places and use different units. Social Security shows a monthly benefit at different claiming ages in today's dollars, a traditional pension shows a monthly amount at the plan's retirement age, the 401(k) and the IRA show account balances before tax, and an annuity shows a contract value.

Two things are always missing from the documents. The first is a check of your **earnings record**. Your Social Security Statement lists the earnings recorded for every year. Missing or wrong years lower the benefit, because it is based on your 35 highest years. Errors should be corrected as early as possible, because the time limit for corrections is generally about three years after the year in question, with exceptions, and old pay slips and W-2 forms become harder to find. The second is the home. It pays no income, but saves rent. This saved rent belongs on the credit side, less property taxes, insurance, maintenance and any mortgage still outstanding at retirement.

bloecke.md:
## Converting to after-tax amounts (step 2)

The individual entitlements are taxed differently. A sum of the account balances and gross amounts therefore says little. Social Security is reduced by the Part B premium, and up to 85% of it can be taxable depending on your other income. Withdrawals from a traditional 401(k) or IRA and pensions are fully taxable; qualified Roth withdrawals are tax-free; from a taxable account, only the gain portion is taxed, often at 0% or 15%.

The differences are large enough to reverse decisions. For example, $500,000 in a traditional IRA and $500,000 in a Roth IRA are two clearly different amounts in the plan, because the first still contains the income tax that will be due on withdrawal.

bloecke.md:
The first misconception concerns the account balance. A balance in a traditional 401(k) or IRA is not all yours. Part of it belongs to the federal government and, in most states, to the state, because every withdrawal is taxed as income. Anyone who compares a traditional balance directly with a Roth balance or a taxable account overestimates the traditional one by their future tax rate.

The second misconception is deflating Social Security twice. The estimates in the Social Security Statement are already expressed in today's dollars; the statement assumes that you continue to work at your current earnings until claiming. If these amounts are reduced again for inflation until retirement, the plan counts the loss of purchasing power twice and underestimates the benefit considerably.

## From the gap to the target capital (step 3)

Need minus entitlements gives the monthly gap, after tax and in today's dollars. To calculate a target capital from it, you need a capital multiple. It states how much wealth one dollar of monthly withdrawal ties up, and it is the reciprocal of the assumed withdrawal percentage, multiplied by twelve. Which percentage is realistic cannot be set freely in the planning; it depends on the withdrawal strategy and the remaining life expectancy. Sound calculations use values between 3% and 4%. If the capital lies mainly in traditional accounts, the gap has to be grossed up by the tax on the withdrawals first.

bloecke.titel: Capital multiple and wealth per dollar of monthly withdrawal

bloecke.md:
Claiming Social Security at 70 instead of at the full retirement age of 67 costs 36 monthly payments. With a benefit of $2,665.80 at 67, that is $95,969. In return, the benefit rises by 24% to $3,305.59, that is, by $639.79 a month for life, adjusted for inflation every year. For the same $639.79 from a portfolio, around $219,000 of capital is needed at a withdrawal rate of 3.5%. Arithmetically, the delay is therefore less than half as expensive. In return, you give up inheritability and availability; measured purely in nominal terms, the forgone payments are made up after about 12.5 years, at around 82½.

The delay is worth most for the higher earner of a married couple, because the surviving spouse keeps the higher of the two benefits, and for anyone in good health. It is worth least for single people with a short life expectancy and for anyone who would have to sell stocks at a low point to bridge the years until 70.

bloecke.formel:
Savings contribution = (gap × F − V × (1 + r)^n) ÷ S

F = 12 ÷ withdrawal percentage
S = ((1 + r/12)^(12n) − 1) ÷ (r/12)
bloecke.erklaerung: The first term is the target capital, the second the amount to which today's assets grow by retirement without further contributions. Only the difference has to be saved.

bloecke.beispiel: Aged 45, 22 years until 67, gap $1,500, F = 343, V = $120,000, r = 3% real. The target capital is $514,500. The existing assets grow to 120,000 × 1.03^22 = $229,900. This leaves $284,600, which with the savings factor S = 373 gives a savings contribution of $762 a month. It is calculated in real terms and is increased annually by inflation.

bloecke.md:
## Order of savings goals (step 4)

This fixes the savings contribution as a figure. Where it goes depends first on what can destroy the plan, and only then on the expected return. An emergency fund prevents a car repair from forcing you to sell investments after a price slump or to run up credit card debt. Disability insurance protects the earned income from which the entire savings contribution comes; according to the Social Security Administration, just over one in four of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before reaching full retirement age. Only after that does return come into play, starting with contracts into which someone else also pays.

bloecke.unter: The order ranks risks and not products. First, whatever can destroy the plan is secured; then comes whatever accelerates wealth building.

bloecke.md:
A match of, say, 50% on contributions up to 6% of salary is an immediate return that no asset class offers. Not contributing enough to receive the full match leaves part of your pay unclaimed. Before relying on it, check the vesting schedule: employer contributions may vest over up to three years with cliff vesting or six years with graded vesting, so leaving the job early can cost part of the match. Your own contributions are always fully vested.

For small incomes, there are two further points. The Saver's Credit reduces the tax by 10%, 20% or 50% of up to $2,000 of contributions to an IRA or workplace plan, depending on income. And for people with very low earnings, Social Security already replaces a large share of income, while savings may count against means-tested benefits such as SSI and Medicaid. A Roth account, whose money can be withdrawn without tax, keeps flexibility in this case.

## Three model plans (step 5)

The three model households each assume a retirement at 67, a real return of 3% and a capital multiple of 343. The need is estimated from today's expenses less saving, payroll taxes, work-related costs and, as a rule, the mortgage payment, which fall away. Expenses for health and housing, by contrast, remain.

bloecke.md:
The example of the 55-year-old shows the problem of planning late. His gap is not the largest of the three, but his savings contribution of $929 is, because he lacks the years in which the capital grows through compound interest. From age 50, he can contribute an additional $8,000 a year to a 401(k) and, at 60 to 63, $11,250, but only if the money is there. If this amount cannot be raised, three options remain, of which the third is the worst.

The first is to work and claim later. Each additional working year has a threefold effect: one year less of withdrawals, one more year of contributions, and a higher Social Security benefit, both because a low earnings year may be replaced in the 35-year average and because each year of delay raises the benefit. Before full retirement age, the reduction for early claiming is 6⅔% a year for the first three years; after it, each year of delay adds 8% up to 70. The second is to reduce the need, most effectively through housing costs, which are the largest and least changeable item in retirement. The third is to take more risk. With twelve years to go, the result can then no longer be planned reliably, because after a price slump there is not enough time for a recovery.

## Regular review

A plan that is calculated once and then filed away is out of date after five years. The method remains valid, but the inputs change, such as salary, children, tax law, contribution limits and interest rates. How often a quantity is reviewed should therefore depend on how quickly it changes, and not on the calendar.

schritte.text: Download the Social Security Statement, file the account statements and update the total of entitlements. Raise the savings contribution by the inflation rate and to the new contribution limits, because otherwise the real calculation turns into a nominal one without anyone noticing. Check the beneficiary designations on all accounts.

schritte.text: Re-estimate the need, check the capital multiple and the return assumption, and recalculate the gap and the savings contribution from scratch. From your mid-fifties, add the claiming strategy for Social Security and the Medicare decision at 65.
Check the earnings record in the Social Security Statement year by year and have errors corrected while pay slips and W-2 forms are still available.

Change of job (roll the old 401(k) over directly instead of cashing it out, check vesting), self-employment (solo 401(k) or SEP IRA), marriage, birth, divorce (division of retirement accounts by court order; a marriage of at least ten years can give rise to benefits on the ex-spouse's record), an inheritance (an inherited IRA generally has to be emptied within ten years).

bloecke.md:
- Gross and net are confused. The Social Security estimate is before the Part B premium and before any income tax, and a traditional 401(k) balance is before income tax.
- The savings contribution is never increased. At 2% inflation, a contribution of $452 has the purchasing power of only $217 after 37 years. In a real calculation, the contribution must therefore rise in nominal terms, in the example to around $940 in the last year.
- The home is valued too highly. The saved rent counts, but less property taxes, insurance, maintenance and any remaining mortgage. Long-term care costs cannot be paid from a house you live in without selling it or borrowing against it.
- A 401(k) is cashed out when changing jobs. Before 59½, this generally costs the income tax plus an additional 10% tax, and the money is missing from the plan. A direct rollover to the new plan or an IRA keeps the tax advantage.
- The spouse is forgotten. Two separate plans do not yet make a household plan. Survivor benefits, the claiming ages of both spouses and the question of who lives on what after the first death belong in the same plan.

The plan assumes a steady return. However, success depends more on the order of returns in the first years of retirement than on their average. A single figure in the plan cannot capture this; a simulation is needed for that.

It also assumes current law. The 2025 Social Security Trustees Report projects that the retirement trust fund (OASI) will be depleted in 2033; after that, incoming payroll taxes would cover about 77% of scheduled benefits unless Congress acts. Congress has changed benefits, taxes and retirement ages before, and it can be assumed that it will act, but not how. Tax law also changes: the brackets made permanent in 2025 can be changed again by any later law. For planning, this means estimating Social Security cautiously, for example with a moderate haircut for younger workers, and not building the plan on a political assumption.

mitnehmen: Need, entitlements, assets and savings contribution must all be stated after tax and in the same purchasing power, that is, either in real terms throughout or in nominal terms throughout.
Account balances cannot be compared directly, because a traditional 401(k) or IRA still contains the income tax due on withdrawal, while Roth money and the basis in a taxable account do not.
The target capital is the gap multiplied by the capital multiple, and at a withdrawal rate of 3.5%, every dollar of monthly income ties up around $343 of wealth.
Every additional dollar is allocated according to risk, in this order: emergency fund, expensive debt, earning capacity, employer match, HSA and IRA, rest of the 401(k) and taxable account.

Starting twenty years later triples the required savings contribution, and if you start late, working and claiming Social Security later and lower housing costs have a stronger effect than a higher stock allocation.

begriffe.text: Wealth tied up by one dollar of monthly withdrawal. The multiple is twelve divided by the assumed withdrawal percentage and, at 3.5%, amounts to around $343 per dollar of monthly income.
Share of the estimated need in retirement that is already covered by entitlements acquired. The remainder is the gap from which the target capital is derived.

Overview from the Social Security Administration with the recorded earnings for every year and estimated benefits at different claiming ages, in today's dollars. It is available online at any time and is mailed to people aged 60 and over who do not yet receive benefits and have no online account.
Employer contribution to a 401(k) or similar plan that depends on the employee's own contribution, for example 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary. It may vest over several years.

The point from which employer contributions to a retirement plan belong to the employee for good. Under federal law, matching contributions must vest within three years (cliff) or six years (graded); the employee's own contributions are always fully vested.
